**Periyar Nature Preserve**

There is no crumbly frozen cake to thaw. Today, we are in the jungle. I mean mosquitoes. I mean tigers and elephants sludging their way to the lake for a drink, and *don’t make sudden moves*, or snakes startled from an afternoon nap will greet you fang-first.

I think we are lost.

It is too hot for any cold confection to survive. Even my tube of sunblock is as warm as a baby’s bottle. You get to those places I can’t reach, those places I dared not even whisper about before I walked down the aisle in white.

You never worried if our families would clash, if they would clang like the clutch of pale monkeys rattling the thin branches of the treetops, begging for our trail mix. You never worried about my relatives staring at your pale, muscled calves—things not usually seen outside the bedroom. You wore hiking shorts anyway. And still, they lavished ladlefuls of food onto your plate.

I think we are lost.

My eyes are dark and wet as that wild deer that walked right past us, a little off the trail. I think we are lost, but for once, I don’t mind.

Eventually, you turn us back toward a place not on any map, but I know I can trace it with my finger if we ever need it again. We made it one year without a compass, and we’re not about to start now.

**Periyar Nature Preserve**

There is no melting slab of frozen dessert waiting for us here.  
Today, we have come into the forest.  
Or rather, into the mosquitoes.  
Or into the land where tigers and elephants push through the mud toward the lake to drink, where a single sharp movement might rouse a snake from its drowsy afternoon coil and bring its fangs out first.

I believe we have lost the trail.

It is far too hot for anything sweet and frozen to remain intact. Even the sunscreen in my tube has heated to the temperature of milk warmed for an infant.

You reach the parts of me I cannot reach myself, the places I would not have dared to name before I stood in white and walked toward you. You never seemed afraid that our two families might collide, might rattle against one another like those pale monkeys shaking the narrow treetop branches while pleading for our trail mix. You never fretted over my relatives noticing your light, strong calves—body parts they were not accustomed to seeing anywhere but behind bedroom doors. Still, you put on your hiking shorts. And still, they heaped your plate with generous spoonful after spoonful of food.

I think we are lost.

My eyes are dark and shining, like the wild deer that passed near us, just beyond the path.

I think we are lost, and for the first time, I am not troubled by it.

At last, you lead us back—not to any place marked on a map, but to somewhere I know I could find again, tracing the route with my finger if we ever had to return. We have managed an entire year without a compass, and we are not going to begin using one now.

In Periyar Nature Preserve, the path disappeared almost as soon as we began to trust it.

At first it had seemed clear enough: a narrow trail pressed into the damp earth, bordered by glossy leaves and roots that rose like knuckles from the ground. We followed our guide through the green hush of the jungle, stepping over vines, ducking under branches, trying not to slip on the dark mud where the morning rain had collected. Somewhere far off, a langur called into the trees. Birds flashed and vanished before we could name them. The forest was alive with movement, but little of it revealed itself directly. It rustled, cracked, breathed, and watched.

We had come to Periyar during the first year of our marriage, still learning the geography of each other. Marriage, we were discovering, was not the tidy joining of two lives we had imagined. It was not simply a ceremony, a shared home, a set of rings, or a promise made in front of people who loved us. It was a daily passage through unfamiliar country. We carried into it different customs, different assumptions, different loyalties, different languages of affection and obligation. Our families had welcomed us, questioned us, worried over us, advised us, blessed us, and, at times, bewildered us. Even love, which had once seemed like the clearest thing in the world, now had to find its way through expectations we had not known how to anticipate.

So when we realized we were lost in the jungle, it felt less like an interruption to our trip than an exaggeration of the life we were already living.

The guide stopped first. He lifted his hand, and we stopped behind him. He looked left, then right, then at the ground, then toward a gap between trees that seemed no different from any other gap. The forest closed around us with calm indifference. There was no dramatic announcement, no thunderclap, no sudden evidence of danger. Only a pause that lasted too long.

“Maybe this way,” he said.

Maybe.

We followed.

The jungle in Periyar did not resemble the maps we had seen at the visitor center. On paper, the preserve had boundaries, trails, lakes, ridges, marked distances, reasonable proportions. Inside it, everything multiplied. Each tree stood among hundreds of other trees. Each path divided into animal tracks, dry streambeds, and places where leaves had merely been flattened by rain. The air smelled of wet bark, soil, and something musky, as if the animals had passed just before us and left the idea of themselves behind.

We saw signs of them everywhere. Hoofprints softened by water. Claw marks on bark. The dark, rounded evidence of elephants. Once, our guide pointed to a broken bamboo stalk and whispered that a gaur had been there. Another time he stopped us near a clearing and tilted his head toward a sound we could barely hear: the low shifting of something large beyond the trees. We stood still, suddenly aware of our bodies, our breath, the smallness of our plans.

I wanted certainty. I wanted the guide to say, “This is the way back.” I wanted him to point with confidence. I wanted the trail to reappear under our feet, undeniable and official. Instead, he kept choosing from a series of possibilities. We moved forward because standing still did not seem like an option.

That, too, felt familiar.

In our marriage, we had already discovered how often we were expected to know where we were going. Which holidays would we spend with which family? Whose traditions would we keep? What language would we speak to future children we did not yet have? How much should we bend toward the past, and how much should we invent for ourselves? There were no neutral answers. Every choice seemed to tug on someone’s memory, someone’s sacrifice, someone’s idea of what a good son, daughter, husband, or wife should do.

Before we married, we had spoken about these things as if conversation itself could become a compass. We believed that if we loved each other well and explained ourselves carefully, we could avoid losing our way. But the first year taught us that love does not prevent confusion. Sometimes it leads you more deeply into it, because now another person’s fears, hopes, and histories are tied to your own. You cannot simply walk out alone.

In the forest, my husband reached back for my hand when the path narrowed. It was a small gesture, almost practical. The mud was slick. Leeches clung to wet leaves. Thorny branches caught at our sleeves. But when he took my hand, I felt something in me settle. He did not know the way either. That was the strange comfort of it. He was not leading me out with superior knowledge. He was lost beside me.

We crossed a shallow stream by stepping from stone to stone. On the other side, the guide hesitated again. The canopy thickened overhead, turning the daylight green. A giant squirrel leapt between branches, its rust-colored body bending like a flame. Somewhere above us, unseen birds made metallic calls. The forest seemed less like a place than a language we could not read. Every sound meant something, but not to us.

“Are we close?” I asked.

The guide smiled without answering directly. “We will come.”

It was not the reassurance I wanted, but it was perhaps the only honest one.

We will come.

Not soon. Not certainly. Not by the route expected. But eventually, if we kept moving, if we paid attention, if we did not panic.

There were moments during that first year when I wished someone could give us a map of marriage—not the sentimental kind, but a real one, with warnings and alternate routes. Here is where pride will make you turn too sharply. Here is where silence becomes a swamp. Here is where your families’ love will feel like pressure. Here is where old grief appears disguised as anger. Here is where you must stop and drink water. Here is where you must apologize before you understand everything. Here is where you must hold hands.

But no such map existed. Or if it did, it could not be drawn by anyone outside the marriage. The terrain was made by our particular lives meeting: his childhood and mine, his country and mine, his inherited rituals and my private rebellions, his ways of enduring discomfort and my ways of naming it. We could ask for advice, and we did. We could listen to our parents, and sometimes we did. But no one else could walk the exact trail for us.

At some point in Periyar, after another uncertain turn, we began to laugh. Not because the situation was funny exactly, but because fear had become too heavy to carry without relief. We were sweating through our clothes. Our shoes were caked with mud. The guide had stopped pretending that the route was obvious. I had twigs in my hair. My husband’s glasses kept fogging in the damp heat. We looked at each other and laughed with the exhausted intimacy of people who have lost the illusion of control.

That laughter changed the forest. It did not make us less lost, but it made being lost feel less like failure. We were still surrounded by trees, still unsure of the way back, still dependent on a guide who seemed to be navigating by instinct and memory rather than any visible sign. Yet something had loosened. We were no longer waiting for certainty before allowing ourselves to be all right.

Maybe that was the lesson the jungle offered: not that we would always find the path quickly, but that we could remain together while searching.

Eventually, the trees thinned. Light opened ahead of us. The ground grew firmer. We saw, with disproportionate joy, a stretch of trail that looked used by human feet. Then came the pale glimmer of water through the branches, and beyond it the wider world: the lake, the boats, the voices of other visitors, the ordinary reassurance of signs and railings and schedules.

We had not been lost forever. We had not been lost beyond repair. We had only been lost long enough to learn what it felt like to continue without guarantees.

Later, when we told the story, we made it sound simpler than it had felt. We got lost in Periyar, we said. Our guide lost the trail. We wandered for hours. We saw monkeys, birds, elephant tracks. We found our way back.

All of that was true. But it was not the whole truth.

The whole truth was that, in the jungle, I understood something about our marriage that I had not understood at the wedding, when everything had been arranged and witnessed and blessed. I understood that vows are not a map. They do not tell you where to turn. They do not remove uncertainty or prevent fear. They are more like the decision to keep walking together after the path has vanished.

We would be lost again, of course. Not in Periyar, perhaps, but in other ways. We would lose our way in conversations about money, family, distance, grief, belonging. We would misunderstand each other. We would disappoint people we loved. We would choose one tradition and feel the ache of another left behind. We would stand, again and again, in the dense green confusion of a shared life and ask, “Are we close?”

And perhaps the answer would often be the same: We will come.

Not because we knew exactly how.

Because we trusted each other enough to keep going.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem titled “Periyar Nature Preserve” about a married couple hiking in an Indian jungle on their first anniversary, blending humor, sensual intimacy, family/cultural tension, and the repeated line “I think we are lost.”
counterfactuals.output:
# Periyar Nature Preserve

On our first anniversary we entered the jungle with two bottles of water, one packet of banana chips, and the kind of confidence only newlyweds possess before noon. The guide had said the path was simple: follow the red earth, listen for langurs, don’t touch anything that looks like it has opinions. You wore your blue scarf, the one my mother said was too bright for the forest and my aunt said was too modern for a wife and my cousin said made you look like a film heroine, which you accepted as the only useful comment in the room.

The air was wet as a kiss. Pepper vines climbed the trees like gossip. Cardamom breathed from the dark. Somewhere beyond the teak and bamboo, an elephant cracked a branch with the leisurely authority of an uncle clearing his throat before giving advice.

“I think we are lost,” you said.

I said no, no, the lake is this way, because husbands on anniversaries are legally required to pretend they understand geography. You looked at the trail, then at me, then at the trail again, and smiled with the mercy of a woman who has seen me assemble a shoe rack upside down.

We walked deeper. Leeches waved from leaves like tiny priests offering blessings we did not want. A giant squirrel flashed rust and gold above us, extravagant as wedding silk. My phone showed no signal, which felt like the jungle had taken away our relatives one by one: your mother’s reminders about turmeric milk, my father’s weather updates, the family WhatsApp group where someone was always sending a good-morning lotus with the emotional weight of a subpoena.

“I think we are lost,” you said again, softer this time, almost laughing.

I wanted to say: yes, perhaps. I wanted to say: I have been lost since the first time you unpinned your hair in my rented apartment and the room became a monsoon. Since you stood beside me under marigolds and temple bells and everyone watched to see whether our love would behave properly. Since your father held my hand too tightly and said, Take care of her, as if love were a government job with benefits and inspections. Since my mother cried into her jasmine and later asked if you would learn our recipes, as though cumin could be citizenship.

Instead I said, “The map is just being abstract.”

You snorted, and the jungle startled. Birds lifted from a fig tree like thrown handfuls of ink.

We stopped where the path split into three red tongues. Sweat shone along your throat. A curl stuck to your cheek. I wanted to touch you there, and did, with one finger, wiping away a drop of rain or desire or both. You leaned into my hand for exactly one second—long enough to ruin me, short enough to be respectable if any hornbill was reporting back to our families.

The forest smelled of damp bark, wild ginger, animal musk, and the secret salt of your skin. You took the last banana chip and placed half on my tongue like prasad. Marriage, I thought, is this: getting half the snack and all the blame.

“I think we are lost.”

“Yes,” I said at last.

The word opened like a clearing.

We sat on a fallen log furred with moss. Above us, the canopy stitched the sky into green fragments. You removed your shoes and cursed delicately at a leech, calling it a freeloading cousin, which made me love you with an almost painful precision. I checked your ankle; you checked mine. Our knees touched. Somewhere in the trees a macaque screamed as if it had just received our wedding expenses.

You rested your head on my shoulder. “My mother will say this is why people should go to Munnar and take photographs with tea bushes.”

“My mother will say you should have packed more food.”

“You will say?”

I looked at you: wife, accomplice, stormlamp, the woman my family tried to understand through customs and menus, the woman your family tried to protect from my insufficient savings and suspiciously poetic career. One year married, and already we had learned that love is not the opposite of inheritance. It is what grows through it, stubborn as a root splitting stone.

“I will say,” I told you, “that the tiger respected our privacy.”

You laughed so hard you fell against me, and for a moment the jungle turned domestic. The bamboo became curtains. The lake, wherever it was, became a rumor of silver beyond the walls. Your hand found mine, mud-streaked, ringed, warm. I kissed your knuckles, then your wrist, tasting rain and salt and the faint sweetness of the banana chip. You closed your eyes. The forest listened with its thousand green ears and, for once, kept quiet.

“I think we are lost,” you whispered, but now the sentence had changed. It no longer meant panic. It meant we had slipped the net of advice, the timetable, the anniversary lunch reservation, the correct pose for photographs. It meant no one knew exactly where we were, and therefore no one could tell us how to be.

At last we rose, following a sound that might have been water, or wind, or the world rinsing itself clean. The trail bent. Light gathered. Through the trees, Periyar Lake appeared suddenly, bright and patient, holding the sky in its animal arms.

You squeezed my hand. “See? I found it.”

“Yes,” I said. “I was following you the whole time.”

This was not true, but it was truer than the map.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person flash nonfiction-style piece set in Periyar Nature Preserve, where the narrator reflects on marriage, interracial/international family dynamics, and getting lost on a hot jungle hike with their spouse.
counterfactuals.output:
At Periyar Nature Preserve, the trail narrowed until it seemed less like a path than a rumor the jungle had once told and then forgotten. My shirt clung to my back. Sweat ran into the corners of my mouth and turned everything salty—my lips, my mood, my marriage.

My husband walked ahead of me, ducking under a vine. He had the map in one hand and the serene expression of a man who believed the world would eventually rearrange itself around his confidence.

“This can’t be right,” I said.

He turned, smiling as if heatstroke were a charming local custom. “It’s fine. We’re close.”

Close to what, I wanted to ask. Close to enlightenment? Close to divorce? Close to becoming a cautionary tale told by park rangers to pale, overprepared tourists and Indian sons visiting from abroad with wives who packed too much water and not enough patience?

We had come to Kerala because his family said it was time I saw “real India,” as if the India I knew through airport embraces, WhatsApp blessings, wedding rituals, and his mother’s careful instruction on how to temper mustard seeds was only a rehearsal. My own family, across the ocean, had asked if I was nervous. About the food? The snakes? The relatives? They meant well, which is to say they meant badly in familiar ways.

Marriage, when it crosses countries, is always being translated. Not just language, but silence. Not just religion, but weather. In his family’s home, love arrived as second helpings, as aunties correcting my sari pleats, as cousins laughing too quickly when I mispronounced Malayalam. In mine, love was privacy, directness, saying “Are you okay?” and expecting an honest answer. We spent years learning that neither side was cold, only fluent in different temperatures.

Now we were lost in one of the hottest places I had ever been, surrounded by bamboo, teak, bird calls like metal scraping glass. Somewhere in the distance, a langur screamed. The forest smelled of wet bark and elephant dung and green things cooking in the sun.

My husband stopped at a fork in the trail.

I stared at him.

He stared at the map.

The map, unlike marriage, offered no emotional nuance. It was simply wrong or we were.

“You don’t know where we are,” I said.

He exhaled. “Not exactly.”

There it was: the tiny sentence every marriage eventually requires. Not exactly. Not the story we told at the wedding. Not the family either of us imagined. Not the country, not the language, not the future we could point to on a paper map and say, Here. We are here.

For a moment I wanted to be furious. I wanted the clean pleasure of blame. He had insisted we didn’t need a guide. He had waved off the park worker’s advice. He had said, with the optimism of his father and the stubbornness of mine, “We’ll manage.”

But then I saw his face—flushed, uncertain, beloved. A man between places. A son returning and still foreign. A husband trying to make a wilderness feel like an inheritance.

I took the water bottle from my bag and handed it to him.

“We’ll manage,” I said, and hated how much it sounded like hope.

We retraced our steps slowly, arguing only a little. At some point the trail widened. A group of hikers appeared, then a signboard sun-bleached and miraculous. Near the preserve entrance, we bought lime sodas from a vendor, cold glass bottles sweating in our hands.

My husband touched his bottle to mine.

“To getting lost,” he said.

I looked past him at the dark edge of the forest, how it held its secrets without apology.

“To being found,” I said.

But I meant: to choosing, again and again, the person beside you when the map fails.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a poetic travel vignette that begins with the phrase “There is no crumbly frozen cake to thaw,” contrasts wedding traditions with a humid wildlife preserve, and ends with the couple deciding they do not need a compass.
counterfactuals.output:
There is no crumbly frozen cake to thaw, no satin ribbon saved in a drawer, no bouquet hung upside down to dry into a brittle relic of luck. The old wedding customs feel far away here, beyond the green throat of the humid wildlife preserve, where the air clings like a second veil and every leaf sweats beneath the afternoon sun.

They walk a boardwalk slick with moss instead of an aisle strewn with petals. Egrets lift like torn handkerchiefs from the reeds. Somewhere, unseen frogs pulse their vows into the mud, and dragonflies stitch blue fire over the dark water. Her dress is linen, his collar open; their rings flash once, briefly, like minnows beneath the surface.

At home, people would have told them what to keep: the top tier of cake, the guest book, the posed photograph under an arch of flowers. Here, the preserve keeps nothing still. Mangrove roots rise like knuckled hands. Orchids bloom without witnesses. A heron steps through the shallows with the solemn grace of an officiant, and the whole wet world seems to pronounce them bound not by ritual, but by breath, heat, and the shared astonishment of arriving.

When the trail forks and the map wilts between their fingers, they laugh softly, listening to the insects, the water, each other. Hand in hand, they decide they do not need a compass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intimate, slightly surreal prose poem about newlyweds in a tiger-and-elephant nature preserve, including sunblock, monkeys, trail mix, exposed calves, relatives feeding the spouse, and the line “I think we are lost.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the tiger-and-elephant preserve, we walked like two people who had promised the future something impossible and were waiting for it to answer.

You had sunblock on your nose, a pale little moon I wanted to kiss off and reapply. I carried trail mix in the pocket nearest my heart, raisins and peanuts knocking together like small weather. The path kept dividing, then pretending it hadn’t. Above us, monkeys moved through the trees with the grave efficiency of old women rearranging a house after a death.

Your calves were exposed beneath your shorts, bright with heat, vulnerable as peeled fruit. I kept looking at them, not from desire exactly, or not only desire, but because marriage had made your body seem newly entrusted to the world. Every thorn had become my business. Every mosquito was a criminal.

At lunch, our relatives appeared as if summoned by blood: aunties in wide hats, uncles damp and shining, cousins carrying metal tiffins, all of them feeding you with their fingers and spoons, pressing mango, rice, sweet lime, fried things into your mouth while I watched with the ceremonial ache of being replaced by everyone who had loved you first.

Somewhere nearby, an elephant broke a branch with the sound of a door opening underwater. Somewhere farther off, the idea of a tiger passed silently through the grass. The monkeys chattered above us, throwing seeds, judgments, tiny green stars.

You took my hand. Your palm was salty from sunblock and saltier from fear.

“I think we are lost.”

The words entered the air and stayed there, striped, enormous. We stood in the heat, married and misdirected, while the preserve breathed around us—leaves lifting, insects ticking, relatives laughing in the distance like a river we might never find again.

Then you smiled, and the whole wild map folded itself smaller.

I gave you the last cashew.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary prose poem titled “Periyar Nature Preserve” in the voice of someone reflecting on their first year of marriage while lost on a jungle trail, using vivid animal imagery and ending with a sense of trust and orientation beyond maps.
counterfactuals.output:
**Periyar Nature Preserve**

In our first year of marriage, I learned how quickly a path can become rumor. One moment we were following the red blazes through cardamom shadow and bamboo clatter, the next the forest had folded itself behind us like a green sari, pleat after pleat, hiding the seam. Leeches worried our socks with their blind persistence. Above us, lion-tailed macaques moved like old thoughts through the canopy, black faces solemn in their silver manes, while a giant squirrel flung its rust-colored body from branch to branch as if the air had promised to catch it.

You said my name the way people say a prayer they don’t fully believe in yet. I answered, and the sound of us was small, two matchsticks struck in the damp cathedral of trees. Somewhere, an elephant cracked bamboo, not loudly, but with the authority of a door closing in another room. We stood still. We had been married eleven months then, still learning which silences meant anger and which meant awe, which hunger was for food and which was for forgiveness.

The map in my pocket had softened with sweat, its lines blurring into blue veins, its legend no longer translating the world. Around us, the jungle kept speaking in bodies: the kingfisher’s electric plunge, the sambar’s sudden bark, the dark script of ants carrying dismantled wings across the trail. A hornbill passed overhead, prehistoric and precise, its beak like a question shaped by patience. I wanted to confess that I had been pretending to know where we were going, not only that afternoon but for months—through rent, rice, sleep, desire, the delicate machinery of two toothbrushes in one cup.

You took my hand without ceremony. Not rescue, not blame. Just the ordinary astonishment of touch. We listened until the forest rearranged itself: water ticking over stone, cicadas sewing heat into the leaves, our breath finding one rhythm and then another. The trail did not appear all at once. It arrived the way trust does, first as a clearing in the chest, then as a brightness between trees. We walked toward it, guided not by the ruined map, but by the river’s low voice and the sure pressure of your palm inside mine.
